The time encoding components
t _ { 1 } , t _ { 2 }
are computed as:
t _ { 1 } = \cos ( \pi t / 1 2 ) \cdot 0 . 5 + 0 . 5
t _ { 2 } = \sin ( \pi t / 1 2 ) \cdot 0 . 5 + 0 . 5\tag{24}
(25)
where 𝑡 represents the current time step within the episode (ranging from 0 to 23 for a 24-hour horizon). The argument
\pi t / 1 2
ensures a full 24-hour period, while the scaling factor of 0.5 ensures that both
t _ { 1 }
and
t _ { 2 }
remain within the range [0, 1], providing normalized temporal representations that capture the periodic nature of daily operational patterns in the DC microgrid. Sinusoidal time encoding captures the periodic nature of daily operational patterns in DC microgrids more effectively than integer representation. Sine and cosine functions naturally represent the 24-hour cyclical patterns of workload demand, electricity prices, renewable generation, and ambient temperature, whereas integer time values do not inherently encode this cyclical relationship. Additionally, sinusoidal encoding provides smooth transitions between adjacent time steps, facilitating gradient-based learning. One-hot encoding, by comparison, creates discontinuous representations that can hinder optimization. The encoding values also remain bounded within [0, 1] after scaling, making them directly compatible with neural network inputs without additional normalization. This encoding approach has since been adapted in various time-series forecasting models [29], demonstrating its effectiveness in capturing temporal dependencies. Note that variables without the time subscript 𝑡
( \mathrm { e . g . , ~ } L ^ { \mathrm { f l x } } , ~ L ^ { \mathrm { i n f l x } } , ~ \lambda ^ { \mathrm { e } } )
represent episode-level data that remain constant throughout the entire episode, while future values beyond the current time step are supplemented by predicted values based on historical patterns and forecasting models. Here, we assume perfect forecasts for workload, ambient temperature, and carbon intensity to establish baseline performance. The robustness analysis under prediction errors is presented in Section 5.6.
3.3 . Action
The action
a _ { t }
is defined as
a _ { t } = \{ a _ { t } ^ { \mathrm { l } } , a _ { t } ^ { \mathrm { c o o l } } , a _ { t } ^ { \mathrm { e s } } \} \in \mathcal { A } ,\tag{26}
where includes workload scheduling action
a _ { t } ^ { \mathrm { l } } \in [ - 1 , 1 ] ,
cooling system action
a _ { t } ^ { \mathrm { c o o l } } \in [ - 1 , 1 ] ,
and energy storage action
a _ { t } ^ { \mathrm { e s } } \in [ - 1 , 1 ] .
The actual control signals executed in the DC microgrid are computed by mapping the normalized action values from the range [−1, 1] to their respective physical control ranges.
